item.title: “Just as, monks, this body subsists in dependence on food, with food as condition it stands; without food it does not stand. So too, monks,…
item.description:
“Just as, monks, this body subsists in dependence on food, with food as condition it stands; without food it does not stand. So too, monks, the five hindrances subsist in dependence on food, with food as condition they stand; without food they do not stand. And what, monks, is the food for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and for the growth and increase of arisen sensual desire? There is, monks, the sign of the beautiful. Frequent unwise attention to it — this is the food for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and for the growth and increase of arisen sensual desire.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.2

item.title: “Furthermore, Cunda, here a person is infatuated, addicted, living surrounded by the five strands of sensual pleasure; that is the fourth kind of pleasure. Cunda,…
item.description:
“Furthermore, Cunda, here a person is infatuated, addicted, living surrounded by the five strands of sensual pleasure; that is the fourth kind of pleasure. Cunda, these four kinds of pleasure are low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, unbeneficial, not leading to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna. Cunda, this is possible: wanderers of other sects might say: ‘The Sakyan ascetics are living addicted to these four kinds of pleasure.’ They should be answered: ‘That is not so; you speak wrongly. You misrepresent us, untruthfully, falsely.’”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 29 – Pāsādikasutta

item.title: “Monks, then I dwelt heedful, ardent, resolute. When a sensual thought arose, I understood: ‘This sensual thought has arisen in me, and it leads to…
item.description:
“Monks, then I dwelt heedful, ardent, resolute. When a sensual thought arose, I understood: ‘This sensual thought has arisen in me, and it leads to my own harm, to others’ harm, to the harm of both, destroys wisdom, is part of vexation, does not lead to Nibbāna.’ Monks, as I reflected: ‘This sensual thought leads to my own harm’ – it subsided. As I reflected: ‘It leads to others’ harm’ – it subsided. As I reflected: ‘It leads to the harm of both’ – it subsided. As I reflected: ‘It destroys wisdom, is part of vexation, does not lead to Nibbāna’ – it subsided. Thus, monks, I continued to remove, abandon, and put an end to sensual thoughts.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 19 – Dvedhāvitakkasutta

item.title: “Through many a birth in samsara I have wandered, Seeking but not finding the builder of this house. Suffering is birth again and again.” “O…
item.description:
“Through many a birth in samsara I have wandered,
Seeking but not finding the builder of this house.
Suffering is birth again and again.”

“O house-builder, you are seen!
You shall not build a house again.
All your rafters are broken,
Your ridge-pole is shattered.
My mind has attained the unconditioned,
And the extinction of craving has been reached.”

From: Dhammapada 146-156

item.title: Elder Eraka: “O Eraka, painful are sensual pleasures! O Eraka, not happiness are sensual pleasures! One who desires sensual pleasures, desires suffering. One who does…
item.description:
Elder Eraka:
“O Eraka, painful are sensual pleasures!
O Eraka, not happiness are sensual pleasures!
One who desires sensual pleasures, desires suffering.
One who does not desire sensual pleasures, does not desire suffering.
O Eraka, know this as it is.”

From: Theragāthā 1.93

item.title: “Householder, having known that sensual desire is a defilement of the mind, that noble disciple abandons sensual desire, the defilement of the mind; having known…
item.description:
“Householder, having known that sensual desire is a defilement of the mind, that noble disciple abandons sensual desire, the defilement of the mind; having known that ill-will is a defilement of the mind, he abandons ill-will; having known that sloth and torpor are defilements of the mind, he abandons sloth and torpor; having known that restlessness and remorse are defilements of the mind, he abandons restlessness and remorse; having known that doubt is a defilement of the mind, he abandons doubt. This, householder, is called a noble disciple of great wisdom, of broad wisdom, who has entered the sphere of clear vision, endowed with wisdom. This is called being endowed with wisdom.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.61
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Elder Nun Selā: You will not escape, You will not escape this world. What use is this practice of seclusion to you? Enjoy sensual pleasures…
item.description:
Elder Nun Selā:

You will not escape,
You will not escape this world.
What use is this practice of seclusion to you?
Enjoy sensual pleasures —
Do not have regrets later.

Sensual pleasures are like swords and spears —
They cut the aggregates to pieces.
What you call the pleasure of life —
For me, that sensual pleasure
Is no longer enticing.

Everywhere, delight is destroyed.
The mass of darkness,
The blinding darkness, has been shattered.
Know this, O Evil One —
You are Māra,
You are defeated.

From: Therīgāthā 3.7
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: - “Venerable sir, do you know the release, the escape, the seclusion for beings?” - “Friend, I know the release, the escape, the seclusion for…
item.description:
- “Venerable sir, do you know the release, the escape, the seclusion for beings?”
- “Friend, I know the release, the escape, the seclusion for beings.”
- “But how, venerable sir, do you know the release, the escape, the seclusion for beings?”
The destruction of delight in renewed existence,
The cessation of perception and consciousness,
The stilling of feelings —
Thus, friend, I know the release,
The escape and seclusion
For all kinds of beings.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.2
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye—these are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing.…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye—these are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. Sounds cognizable by the ear … Odors cognizable by the nose … Tastes cognizable by the tongue … Tangibles cognizable by the body—these are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. These, monks, are the five strands of sensual pleasure.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta
